title: Agency reasons, litigation explanations, and remand
shortTitle: Agency reasons, litigation explanations, and remand
summary: Judicial review normally evaluates the rationale the agency adopted; a court must remand when sustaining the result would require an unmade administrative judgment.
notes:
The Chenery I principle requires an agency to disclose reasons that a reviewing court can assess and that actually support the exercise of authority. Litigation counsel cannot replace an erroneous legal premise with an administrative policy judgment the agency never made. The principle simultaneously permits legal review and protects the agency’s assigned discretion from judicial substitution.

The notes distinguish clarification or harmless error from a new discretionary justification. Wyman-Gordon describes an unusually certain outcome for which remand would be an idle formality. Calcutt v. FDIC confines that exception to narrow circumstances: a court could not repair legal errors within a larger discretionary sanction decision by predicting the same outcome. The proper response was to identify the legal errors and return the discretionary choice to the agency. This distinction explains why a confident prediction is generally insufficient and why Chenery does not prohibit an agency itself from reconsidering and giving a lawful explanation on remand.
